html:
The state storehouses of the Inca Empire, called qullqa. Thousands of them stood in rows on hillsides near towns and along the roads, placed where cold wind and dry air helped keep food from rotting.

They held chuño, a freeze-dried potato that keeps for years, along with maize, dried llama meat, cloth, sandals and weapons. Keepers counted everything on quipus.

The stores fed armies on the march and the people who came to work for the state under the mit'a labour duty. In bad years they could help feed people in hard-hit areas. They let the Inca run a large state without money or markets.

When the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, they found many storehouses full, and the stores helped feed both sides in the wars that followed. Ruins of them survive at sites like Huánuco Pampa and Cotapachi.
